introduction-the-bouncer-at-the-door.core: A rate limiter caps how many requests a client may make in a time window, protecting shared capacity from abuse, runaway clients and accidental floods. It needs an identity to key on (API key, user, IP), a rule (for example 100 requests per minute), an algorithm to count, and a response for violators, usually HTTP 429 with Retry-After.

first_principles.problem: One customer's buggy retry loop sends 50,000 requests per second and degrades the API for everyone.
truths: Limits need identity and a clock.

analogy.title: A bouncer counting people in
analogy.story: He lets people in at a steady pace and turns away anyone once the room is full, telling them when to try again.
analogy.breaks: Bouncers judge faces; limiters apply exact rules per key.

example.title: Fixed window counter

steps.label: Weakness
steps.detail: 200 requests can pass across a window boundary in 2 seconds.

example.outcome: a basic limiter and its flaw.

check.q: What is the boundary problem with fixed windows?
check.a: A client can use the full limit at the end of one window and again at the start of the next, doubling the burst.

the-leaky-bucket-smooth-and-steady.core: The leaky bucket treats requests as water poured into a bucket with a hole: it drains at a fixed rate no matter how fast water arrives. Requests are queued (or counted) and processed at a constant outflow; when the bucket is full, new arrivals are dropped. The output is perfectly smooth, which protects downstream systems but adds queueing delay and doesn't allow bursts.

first_principles.problem: A legacy payment gateway falls over if it receives more than 10 calls per second, even briefly.

analogy.title: A funnel into a bottle
analogy.story: Pour as fast as you like; it only flows out at the funnel's rate, and it overflows if you pour too much.
analogy.breaks: Water spills messily; requests get a clean rejection.

example.title: NGINX limit_req

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Gateway sees a steady 10 req/s; excess beyond 20 queued gets 503/429.

example.outcome: smoothed traffic for a fragile backend.

check.q: What does the leaky bucket trade for smooth output?
check.a: Latency (requests wait in the queue) and the inability to serve legitimate bursts quickly.

the-token-bucket-bursts-allowed.core: A token bucket refills with tokens at a fixed rate up to a maximum capacity. Each request spends a token; if none are left it's rejected or delayed. An idle client accumulates tokens, so it can burst up to the capacity, while the long-run average stays bounded by the refill rate. It is easy to implement lazily: compute tokens from the elapsed time on each request.

first_principles.problem: A mobile app legitimately sends 20 requests at launch then goes quiet, but a strict 5 req/s limiter rejects most of them.
truths: Average rate and burst are different needs.
derivation: On request: tokens = min(b, tokens + r·Δt).

analogy.title: A transit card topped up automatically
analogy.story: It gains credit every hour up to a cap; you can spend a lot at once if you've saved, but you can't exceed the cap.
analogy.breaks: Cards hold money; tokens are just a computed number.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: rate=5, cap=20: app's 20-request launch burst passes, then 5/s sustained.

check.q: If rate=10/s and capacity=50, what's the max burst after a long idle period?
check.a: 50 requests at once, then 10 per second after that.

leaky-vs-token-the-comparison.core: Both buckets bound the long-run rate, but they shape traffic differently. The leaky bucket shapes output to a constant rate, queueing or dropping bursts: good in front of fragile systems. The token bucket polices input, letting bursts through up to capacity: good for user-facing APIs. Distributed enforcement adds another dimension, using a shared store such as Redis with atomic scripts, or approximate local limits.

first_principles.problem: A team picks the leaky bucket for a public API, and users complain about latency during normal bursty usage.
derivation: At huge scale → **local limits** with periodic sync.

analogy.title: A metronome vs a savings account
analogy.story: The metronome forces a steady beat; the savings account lets you spend saved credit in a lump.
analogy.breaks: Musicians can rush; limiters are exact.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: All API nodes share one consistent bucket per key.

code.text:
-- KEYS[1]=bucket ARGV: rate, cap, now, cost
local b = redis.call('HMGET', KEYS[1], 't', 'ts')
local t  = tonumber(b[1]) or tonumber(ARGV[2])
local ts = tonumber(b[2]) or tonumber(ARGV[3])
t = math.min(tonumber(ARGV[2]), t + (ARGV[3] - ts) * ARGV[1])
local ok = t >= tonumber(ARGV[4])
if ok then t = t - ARGV[4] end
redis.call('HSET', KEYS[1], 't', t, 'ts', ARGV[3])
redis.call('EXPIRE', KEYS[1], 3600)
return ok and 1 or 0

check.q: Which bucket suits protecting a third-party API with a hard 10 req/s cap?
check.a: The leaky bucket, because it guarantees a smooth outflow that never exceeds the cap.
